intro: Judaism, Christianity and Islam are three of the world's biggest religions. They began in the same part of the world. All three tell stories about Abraham. All three teach that there is one God. Millions of people in Chicago follow one of them.

In this unit, you will visit a Passover table, an Easter church, and a Ramadan sunset. You will read short lines from the Torah, the Gospels and the Qur'an. You will learn what each tradition's people believe and do.

By the end, you will be able to name each tradition's holy book and main practices. You will explain what the three share and how they differ. And you will do it the way a scholar does: describe, do not judge.
bigQuestion: How are Judaism, Christianity and Islam alike, and how are they different?

title: Judaism, Christianity and Islam

chapters.title: Abraham's Family: Judaism and Christianity
chapters.bigQuestion: How can two traditions share old stories and still believe different things?

story.title: Two Tables, One Story
story.kicker: Two cousins sit at two different holiday tables in the same spring week, and both hear about Moses.
paragraphs: Maya and Leo are cousins. They live in Chicago, two streets apart. Maya's family is Jewish. Leo's family is Christian. One spring week, both families get ready for a big holiday meal.

At Maya's house, it is Passover. The table has a special plate. It holds a bone, bitter herbs, and a green vegetable. There is flat bread called matzah. Maya's grandpa reads from a book called the Haggadah. It tells how Moses led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt.

A few days later, Leo's family eats an Easter dinner. Before the meal, they went to church. The pastor talked about Jesus. She also read the story of Moses and the escape from Egypt. Leo is surprised. "That's Maya's story too!" he whispers.

The next day, the cousins compare notes. Both families know Moses. Both read the same old books. But Leo's family also reads books about Jesus. Maya's family does not see those books as part of their Bible. "So we share some stories," Maya says. "But not all of them."
story.think: What did Maya and Leo find out that their families share, and what did they find out is different?

sections.title: The Story of the Jewish People

lessons.title: Abraham and One God
lessons.mainIdea: Jews, Christians and Muslims all tell stories about Abraham, who Jews see as the first of their ancestors.
reading: The Hebrew Bible tells a story about a man named *Abraham*. It says God told him to leave his home and go to a new land. God promised to make his family into a great people. Jewish tradition calls Abraham the first father of the Jewish people.

In the story, God and Abraham make a *covenant*. A covenant is a serious promise between two sides. Jews believe God promised to care for Abraham's family. Abraham's family promised to follow God. Jews believe this promise still links them to God today.

Abraham is important to Christians and Muslims too. That is why Judaism, Christianity and Islam are sometimes called the Abrahamic religions. All three teach that there is only one God. But each tradition tells Abraham's story in its own way.

words.d: a man in the Hebrew Bible whom Jews see as the first father of their people
a serious promise between two sides; in the Hebrew Bible, the bond between God and Abraham's family

lessons.title: Moses and Mount Sinai
lessons.mainIdea: Jews tell how Moses led the Israelites out of Egypt and how God gave the Torah at Mount Sinai.
reading: Every spring, Jewish families retell a story at *Passover*. The Torah says the Israelites were slaves in Egypt long ago. A leader named *Moses* asked the king to let them go. In the story, God helped them escape. Passover celebrates that freedom.

After the escape, the story says, the people camped by a mountain called Sinai. Jews believe God gave Moses the Torah there. The Ten Commandments are part of it. They include rules like "Do not steal" and "Honor your father and mother."

At the Passover meal, called a seder, families eat special foods. Flat bread called matzah reminds them the Israelites left in a hurry. Bitter herbs remind them how hard slavery was. Children ask questions, and adults answer with the story.

words.d: the leader who, in the Torah, brings the Israelites out of Egypt and receives God's law at Mount Sinai
a spring Jewish holiday that remembers the Israelites' escape from slavery in Egypt
the special Passover meal, with foods and questions that retell the story

choices: It reminds them the Israelites left in a hurry

check.q: Where do Jews believe God gave Moses the Torah?
check.why: The Torah tells that Moses received God's law at Mount Sinai.

lessons.title: The Torah
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah, the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, is the most important text in Judaism.
reading: In a synagogue, a long scroll is kept in a special cabinet. It is the *Torah*. The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible. A trained writer copies it by hand in Hebrew. People do not touch the letters. They use a pointer called a yad.

The Torah has stories, like Abraham and Moses. It also has laws about how to live. Jews believe these laws teach how to be fair, kind and holy. One law says, "Love your neighbor as yourself." Jewish teachers have explained these laws for thousands of years.

The whole Hebrew Bible has more books than the Torah. It also has books of prophets, poems and wisdom. Jews call the whole collection the *Tanakh*. Christians read these same books. They call them the Old Testament.

words.d: the first five books of the Hebrew Bible; the most important Jewish text
the Jewish name for the whole Hebrew Bible: Torah, Prophets and Writings
a long roll of paper or parchment with writing on it

choices: A book about the life of Jesus

check.q: Why do readers use a pointer called a yad?
choices: To ring a bell at the start of prayer
To mark the date of Passover
So they do not touch the letters of the scroll
check.why: Out of respect, readers follow the Torah's letters with a yad instead of a finger.

check.q: What do Christians call the books Jews call the Tanakh?
check.why: Christians read the same Hebrew books and call them the Old Testament.

lessons.title: The Synagogue and Shabbat
lessons.mainIdea: Many Jews gather at a synagogue and rest on Shabbat, from Friday sunset to Saturday night.
reading: On Friday evening, just before sunset, a family lights two candles. They say a blessing over bread and grape juice or wine. This begins *Shabbat*, the Jewish day of rest. Shabbat lasts until Saturday night, when three stars can be seen.

The Torah says God rested on the seventh day after making the world. It tells people to rest too. Many Jews do not work on Shabbat. They spend time with family, pray, eat together and read. Different families keep Shabbat in different ways.

Many Jews go to a *synagogue* on Shabbat. A synagogue is a Jewish house of prayer and learning. A rabbi is a teacher who leads the community. Jews may be Orthodox, Conservative or Reform. These groups keep the old laws in different ways.

words.d: the Jewish day of rest, from Friday sunset to Saturday night
a Jewish house of prayer, study and gathering
a Jewish teacher who leads a community

look.title: Remember the Sabbath
look.text: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.
look.prompt: This is one of the Ten Commandments. What does it tell people to do?

check.q: When does Shabbat begin?
choices: On the first day of spring
check.why: Shabbat starts on Friday at sunset and ends Saturday night.

check.q: What is a synagogue?

check.why: These are three big movements within Judaism.

lessons.title: Kosher Food and the Jewish Year
lessons.mainIdea: Kosher rules guide what many Jews eat, and holidays like Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur mark the Jewish year.
reading: The Torah has rules about food. Food that follows these rules is called *kosher*. For example, kosher rules do not allow pork. Meat and milk are not eaten together. Some Jews keep every rule. Others keep some or none.

The Jewish year has special days. Rosh Hashanah is the Jewish New Year, in the fall. People eat apples dipped in honey for a sweet year. Ten days later comes *Yom Kippur*. On that day, many adults fast and pray. They ask forgiveness for wrongs they did.

Other holidays remember stories. Hanukkah lasts eight nights in winter. Families light candles on a menorah. They remember a time long ago when, as Jewish tradition tells it, a little oil burned for eight days in the Temple.

words.d: food that follows Jewish food laws from the Torah
the Jewish Day of Atonement, a fall day of fasting and asking forgiveness
the Jewish New Year, celebrated in the fall

check.q: What does kosher mean?

check.why: Kosher food follows the food rules in the Torah.

check.q: What do many Jews eat on Rosh Hashanah to wish for a sweet year?
check.why: Apples and honey are a Rosh Hashanah custom.

check.q: What do many Jewish adults do on Yom Kippur?
check.why: Yom Kippur is a day of fasting, prayer and asking forgiveness.

lessons.title: Jerusalem, a Shared City
lessons.mainIdea: Jerusalem is a holy city for Jews, Christians and Muslims.
reading: In the city of *Jerusalem*, people stand and pray at an old stone wall. It is called the Western Wall. Some push small paper prayers into the cracks. The wall is part of what was left around the Temple, which the Romans destroyed in 70 CE.
For Jews, Jerusalem is the holiest city. Long ago, the Temple stood there. Jews around the world face toward Jerusalem when they pray. Many end the Passover meal by saying, "Next year in Jerusalem."

Jerusalem matters to Christians too. The Gospels say Jesus taught, died and rose there. Muslims also call it a holy city. The Dome of the Rock stands there. People of many faiths live in and visit the city.

words.d: a city holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims
the great house of worship that once stood in Jerusalem, destroyed in 70 CE

look.title: One city, three views
look.text: A Jewish family prays at the Western Wall. A Christian group walks to a church built where many Christians believe Jesus was buried. Muslims pray at al-Aqsa Mosque, near the Dome of the Rock.
look.prompt: Why might one city be so important to three different traditions?

choices: A wall in a church in Rome
A wall in a Chicago synagogue
An old wall from around the Temple where Jews pray
check.why: The Western Wall is what remains around the Temple area in Jerusalem.

check.q: Which traditions call Jerusalem holy?
check.why: All three Abrahamic traditions hold Jerusalem holy.

check.q: Who destroyed the Temple in 70 CE?
check.why: Roman armies destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem in 70 CE.

lessons.title: Jesus the Teacher
lessons.mainIdea: Christians follow Jesus, a Jewish teacher who, the Gospels say, taught about love for God and others.
reading: About 2,000 years ago, a Jewish man named *Jesus* lived in the land of Israel. He was a teacher. The stories of his life are in four books called the *Gospels*. Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God. Jews do not share that belief.

The Gospels say Jesus taught by telling stories. In one, a traveler is hurt on the road. Two important men walk past. Then a Samaritan stops to help. Samaritans and Jews did not get along then. Jesus asks who acted as a real neighbor.

Jesus taught two great rules. Love God with all your heart. Love your neighbor as yourself. Both rules come from the Torah. Christians try to live by them. The Good Samaritan story shows that a neighbor can be anyone who needs help.

words.d: a Jewish teacher; Christians believe he is the Son of God
four books of the Bible about the life and teaching of Jesus
a short story that teaches a lesson

look.title: Go and do the same
look.text: Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves? And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.
look.prompt: Who does the listener say was the real neighbor? What does Jesus tell him to do?

check.q: What are the Gospels?
choices: The first five books of the Hebrew Bible

check.why: The Gospels are the four books that tell about Jesus.

check.q: In the Good Samaritan story, who helps the hurt traveler?
check.why: The Samaritan stops to help, while others walk past.

check.q: Which belief about Jesus do Christians hold and Jews do not?
choices: That Jesus is the Son of God
check.why: Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God; Judaism does not teach this.

lessons.title: Christmas and Easter
lessons.mainIdea: Christmas remembers the birth of Jesus, and Easter celebrates what Christians believe is his rising from death.
reading: In December, many churches set up a small scene. It shows a baby in a manger with his mother, Mary. This is the story of Jesus' birth in Bethlehem. Christians remember it at *Christmas*, on December 25. Some Orthodox churches keep it on January 7.

The Gospels say Jesus was put to death on a cross. Christians believe that three days later he rose from the dead. They celebrate this on *Easter* Sunday. For many Christians, Easter is the most important day of the year.
Easter moves each year. It comes on a Sunday in spring, after a full moon. Before Easter, many Christians keep Lent. Lent is about forty days of prayer. Many give something up during that time.

words.d: the Christian holiday that remembers the birth of Jesus
the Christian holiday that celebrates the belief that Jesus rose from death
about forty days of prayer before Easter

look.title: Why a cross?
look.text: Look at the top of many churches. You will often see a cross. The Gospels say Jesus died on a cross. Christians believe he then rose to life again.
look.prompt: Why do you think the cross became a sign for Christians?

check.q: What does Christmas remember?
check.why: Christmas remembers the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem.

check.q: Why is Easter important to many Christians?
choices: It is the Jewish New Year
It marks the end of Ramadan
They believe Jesus rose from the dead
check.why: Christians celebrate Easter as the day Jesus rose.

check.q: What is Lent?
choices: About forty days of prayer before Easter
check.why: Lent is a season of prayer before Easter.

lessons.title: The Bible's Two Parts
lessons.mainIdea: The Christian Bible has two parts, the Old Testament and the New Testament.
reading: Open a Christian *Bible* and you find two parts. The first is the *Old Testament*. It has the same books as the Hebrew Bible, though the order and number can differ. It tells of Abraham, Moses and the prophets.

The second part is the *New Testament*. It has 27 books. It starts with the four Gospels about Jesus. Then come letters by early Christian leaders, like Paul. These letters gave advice to new churches.

So Jews and Christians share many books. But Jews do not read the New Testament as scripture. This is one big difference. Christians read the old stories as pointing to Jesus. Jews read them as God's teaching for the Jewish people.

words.d: the holy book of Christians, with an Old and a New Testament
the Christian name for the books Jews call the Hebrew Bible
the second part of the Christian Bible, with the Gospels and letters

look.title: Books in the Bible
look.cite: Standard book counts; Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include a few more Old Testament books
look.prompt: Why might the Hebrew Bible count 24 books but a Protestant Old Testament count 39?

check.q: How many books are in the New Testament?
check.why: The New Testament has 27 books.

check.q: Which part of the Christian Bible has the same books as the Hebrew Bible?
check.why: The Old Testament contains the books of the Hebrew Bible.

check.q: Which statement is true?
choices: Jews do not read the Torah
Christians do not read the Old Testament
Jews do not read the New Testament as scripture
The Gospels are in the Torah
check.why: The New Testament is scripture for Christians but not for Jews.

lessons.title: Church, Baptism and Three Families
lessons.mainIdea: Christians gather in churches, share baptism and communion, and belong to three big families: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant.
reading: A baby is dressed in white. A minister pours water on her head. This is *baptism*. Most Christians see it as the way a person joins the church. Some churches baptize babies. Others baptize people when they are older.

At many services, Christians share bread and wine or grape juice. This is *communion*. They believe it remembers Jesus' last meal with his friends. Most Christians meet on Sunday, the day they believe Jesus rose.

Christians belong to three big families. Catholics are led by the pope in Rome. Orthodox churches are strong in Greece, Russia and Eastern Europe. Protestants, like Baptists and Lutherans, formed after the 1500s. Chicago has churches of all three.

words.d: a Christian rite using water that welcomes a person into the church
sharing bread and wine or juice to remember Jesus' last meal
one of the Christian families that formed after the 1500s

check.why: Baptism uses water to welcome someone into the church.

check.q: Who leads the Catholic Church?
check.why: Catholics are led by the pope in Rome.

check.q: What are Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant?
check.why: These are the three largest groups in Christianity.

chapters.title: Islam: One God, Five Pillars
chapters.bigQuestion: How do the Five Pillars shape a Muslim's day and year?

story.title: The Sunset Date
story.kicker: A family waits for the sun to go down on a day in Ramadan.
paragraphs: It is a spring evening in Chicago. Amina is ten. Her family is Muslim, and it is the month of Ramadan. Her parents and her big brother have not eaten or had a drink since before dawn. Amina is fasting for half the day, for practice.
The kitchen smells like soup and warm bread. On the table sits a bowl of dates and a pitcher of water. Everyone watches the clock. Amina's little brother keeps asking, "Is it time yet?"

Then the call to prayer plays from her dad's phone. The sun has set. Amina's mother hands everyone a date. "Bismillah," they say, which means "in the name of God." They eat the sweet date and drink the cool water. This meal is called iftar.

After a few bites, the family stands on their prayer rugs. They pray together, facing toward Mecca. Then they sit down to the big meal. Amina's grandmother says Ramadan helps her remember people who are hungry every day.
story.think: What did Amina's family do at sunset, and why do you think they started with something small?

lessons.title: Muhammad in Mecca
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe Muhammad was the last prophet, and that God first spoke to him through an angel in a cave near Mecca.
reading: Muslims tell the story of *Muhammad*. He was born in Mecca, in Arabia, around 570 CE. His parents died when he was young. He grew up to be a trader known for being honest. People called him "the trustworthy one."

Muhammad often went to a cave on a mountain to think and pray. Muslims believe that one night, in about 610 CE, the angel Gabriel came to him there. The angel brought words from God. Muslims believe Muhammad is God's last *prophet*.

Muhammad began to teach that there is only one God. Some people in Mecca did not like his message. In 622 CE, he and his followers moved to the city of Medina. This move is called the Hijra. The Islamic calendar counts its years from it.

words.d: the man Muslims believe was God's last prophet
a person who, adherents believe, brings a message from God
Muhammad's move from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE

look.title: Moments in Muhammad's life
look.cite: Common dates from Islamic tradition and historians; early dates are approximate
look.prompt: How old was Muhammad, about, when Muslims believe the first message came?

check.q: Where was Muhammad born?
check.why: Muslims tell that Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 CE.

check.q: What is the Hijra?
choices: Muhammad's move from Mecca to Medina
check.why: The Hijra was the move to Medina in 622 CE.

check.q: Who do Muslims believe brought God's words to Muhammad?
check.why: Muslims believe the angel Gabriel brought the first message in the cave.

lessons.title: The Qur'an
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe the Qur'an is God's own words, given to Muhammad in Arabic.
reading: A girl sits with a teacher. She reads aloud from a book in Arabic. Her voice rises and falls like a song. The book is the *Qur'an*, the holy book of Islam. Many Muslims learn to recite parts of it by heart.

Muslims believe the Qur'an holds God's exact words. They believe it was given to Muhammad over about 23 years. It is written in Arabic. Translations help people understand it. But many Muslims say only the Arabic is truly the Qur'an.
The Qur'an has 114 chapters. Each is called a *surah*. One short surah says God is one and has no equal. The Qur'an names many prophets from the Bible, like Abraham, Moses and Jesus.

words.d: the holy book of Islam, which Muslims believe is God's words in Arabic
a chapter of the Qur'an
to say aloud, often from memory

look.title: God is one
look.text: Say: He is God, the One. God, who needs nothing and on whom all depend. He has no child and no parent, and there is nothing like Him.
look.prompt: What does this short surah say about God?

check.q: In what language was the Qur'an given, as Muslims believe?
check.why: Muslims believe the Qur'an was given in Arabic.

check.q: How many surahs does the Qur'an have?
check.why: The Qur'an has 114 surahs, or chapters.

check.q: Which prophets named in the Bible also appear in the Qur'an?
check.why: The Qur'an names many biblical prophets, including Abraham, Moses and Jesus.

lessons.title: Allah Means God
lessons.mainIdea: Allah is the Arabic word for God, used by Muslims and by Arabic-speaking Christians.
reading: Muslims often say "*Allah*." Some people think this is a different name for a different god. But Allah is simply the Arabic word for God. Arabic-speaking Christians also use this word.

The main belief of Islam is *tawhid*. This means God is one. Muslims believe God has no partners and no children. They believe God made everything and cares for it. This belief is at the center of everything Muslims do.

Muslims believe God sent many prophets to teach people. They name Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus. Muslims respect Jesus as a great prophet. But they do not believe he is God's son, as Christians do.

words.d: the Arabic word for God
the Muslim belief that God is one

look.title: Three ways to say God
look.text: A word can change with the language. In English, people say "God." In Spanish, they say "Dios." In Arabic, they say "Allah."
look.prompt: Why might it be wrong to think "Allah" is the name of a different god?

check.q: What does Allah mean?
check.why: Allah is simply the Arabic word for God.

check.q: What is tawhid?
choices: The belief that God is one
check.why: Tawhid is the Muslim belief in the oneness of God.

check.q: How do Muslims see Jesus?
choices: As a great prophet, not God's son
As the writer of the Qur'an
check.why: Muslims honor Jesus as a prophet but do not believe he is God's son.

lessons.title: Saying the Faith and Praying
lessons.mainIdea: The first two pillars are saying the faith and praying five times a day.
reading: Islam has *Five Pillars*. These are five main duties. Like pillars holding up a roof, they hold up a Muslim's life. The first pillar is the *shahada*. A Muslim says, "There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God."

The second pillar is *salat*, or prayer. Muslims pray five times a day: at dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night. Before praying, they wash their hands, face and feet. They face toward the Kaaba in Mecca.
During prayer, Muslims stand, bow and kneel. They touch their foreheads to the floor. Many use a prayer rug. At school or work, a Muslim may need a quiet place for a few minutes to pray.

words.d: the five main duties of Islam
the statement of faith: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is his messenger
the Muslim prayer said five times a day

look.title: A quiet corner

lessons.title: Giving and Fasting
lessons.mainIdea: The third and fourth pillars are giving to people in need and fasting during Ramadan.
reading: The third pillar is *zakat*. It means giving to people in need. Muslims who have enough give a set share of their savings each year, often about 2.5 percent. The money helps the poor, the hungry and others in need.

The fourth pillar is fasting in *Ramadan*. Ramadan is a month in the Islamic calendar. From dawn to sunset, healthy adults do not eat or drink. Children, sick people and travelers do not have to fast. They can join in other ways.

Muslims believe fasting helps them grow closer to God. It helps them feel thankful and remember hungry people. Each evening, families break the fast with iftar. Many start with a date and water, as Muhammad did.

lessons.title: The Pilgrimage to Mecca
lessons.mainIdea: The fifth pillar is the hajj, a journey to Mecca that Muslims make once in their life if they can.
reading: Picture millions of people in plain white clothes. They walk together around a large cube covered in black cloth. The cube is the *Kaaba*, in Mecca. This is the *hajj*, the pilgrimage to Mecca.

The hajj is the fifth pillar. Muslims who are healthy and can afford it try to go once in their lives. The white clothes make everyone look alike. Rich and poor stand side by side. Pilgrims come from every country.
Muslims believe Abraham and his son Ishmael built the Kaaba to worship one God. At the end of the hajj comes Eid al-Adha. It remembers Abraham's faith. Families share meat with friends and the poor.

words.d: the pilgrimage to Mecca, the fifth pillar

lessons.title: The Mosque and Friday Prayer
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims gather at a mosque, and many attend a special group prayer at midday on Friday.
reading: From a tall tower, a voice calls people to prayer. The tower is a minaret. The building is a *mosque*, a Muslim house of prayer. Inside, there are no chairs. People pray in rows on carpets.

One wall has a small arch called the *mihrab*. It shows the direction of Mecca. A leader called an *imam* leads the prayer. Before going in, people take off their shoes. They wash at a fountain or sink.

On Friday at midday, many Muslims go to the mosque for jumu'ah. This is the Friday group prayer. The imam gives a talk, called a khutbah. Chicago has many mosques, such as in Bridgeview and on the North Side.

words.d: a Muslim house of prayer
a person who leads prayer at a mosque

lessons.title: Eid: Two Big Celebrations
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims celebrate two Eids: Eid al-Fitr after Ramadan and Eid al-Adha at the time of the hajj.
reading: When Ramadan ends, families wake up early. They put on new clothes. They go to a big morning prayer, sometimes in a park. Afterward, people hug and say "Eid Mubarak!" This means "blessed celebration." The day is *Eid al-Fitr*.
Eid al-Fitr celebrates the end of the fast. Before the prayer, Muslims give food or money to the poor. Then comes a feast with family and friends. Children often get gifts or money.

The second Eid is *Eid al-Adha*. It comes at the time of the hajj. It remembers the story of Abraham's faith in God. Many families share meat in three parts: for the family, for friends and for the poor.

words.d: the celebration at the end of Ramadan
the celebration at the time of the hajj that remembers Abraham's faith

lessons.title: Sunni and Shia, Near and Far
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims live all over the world, and most are Sunni or Shia, two big families within Islam.
reading: Islam began in Arabia. Today about 1.9 billion Muslims live around the world. The country with the most Muslims is Indonesia, in Asia. Many Muslims also live in Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Egypt, Nigeria and the United States.

After Muhammad died in 632 CE, Muslims disagreed about who should lead them. This led to two big families. *Sunni* Muslims are the larger group, about 85 to 90 percent. *Shia* Muslims are the rest. Many Shia live in Iran and Iraq.

Sunni and Shia share the Qur'an, the Five Pillars and belief in one God. They differ on some leaders and customs. The Chicago area is home to many Muslims. Their families came from South Asia, the Middle East, Africa and beyond, and many are Black Americans.

words.d: the largest family of Muslims
the second-largest family of Muslims, many living in Iran and Iraq
